newsitem.title: JORDAN: Jordanian shares hit year-high on capital tax cut.
newsitem.headline: Jordanian shares hit year-high on capital tax cut.

text.p: Shares on Jordan's stock exchange climbed to their highest level for over a year on Wednesday after parliament approved the scrapping of a 15 percent tax on companies raising capital.
On the final trading day of the Moslem holy month of Ramadan the market shook off its customary lethargy to rise 0.82 percent to 156.17 in turnover of 481,000 dinars ($679,000).
"It was an active market, mainly in reaction to parliament's decision," broker Abdul-Muattalib Abu Hijleh said.
Parliament approved on Tuesday cancellation of the punishing 15 percent levy, charged on transfer of company reserves into capital, as part of a wider overhaul of Jordan's companies law.
The complete law is not likely to pass through parliament until after next week's Moslem Eid holiday, but is not expected to meet any major opposition.
The decision boosted trade in two banks who have said they plan to boost their capital with bonus share issues backed by cash transfers from reserves.
Arab Bank, which is heavily weighted on the official Amman Financial Market's 60-share index, rose 4.50 dinars to a 12-month high of 263 dinars before slipping back to close at 261.50 dinars.
Jordan Islamic Bank, planning a one-for-four bonus share issue to increase its capital, rose 0.06 dinars to 3.96 dinars.
Abu Hijleh said Industrial Development Bank, which rose 0.06 to 2.44 dinars, and Arab Potash, which rose 0.10 dinars, were also expected to benefit from parliament's decision.
Brokers said they also welcomed parliamentary approval for scrapping the state's issuing committee, which sets prices of new share issues.
"Now firms will be able to determine their own share price, without going to the Ministry of Trade and Industry," said Nasser al-Amad, head of United Financial Investments.

Jordanian banks must comply by the end of the year with a Central Bank ruling to increase their capital bases to at least 20 million dinars ($28.2 million). But many have indicated they plan to raise the money through private share placements, which would not have been liable to the 15 percent tax.
Fund managers say foreign buying on the Amman stock exchange has picked up in the last two months on hopes of further economic reforms and sales of state-owned stock in 1997.
Overall 19 shares rose on Wednesday and just two fell. Shares in another 12 companies traded but closed unchanged. The market will be closed for the Eid holiday until next Wednesday.
